posts.name: phantaskippy
posts.cooked:
To me the key to Harpy is managing and setting up swings between Arcane and Avian tokens.  Don't just sit on one side until you run out of cards for that style and then not be able to swing to the other side.  Your cards that flip tokens are huge, use them wisely and often holding onto them until it is time to switch sides is key.

Pay attention to when thigs happen.  Conjured Aura checks for destruction at the start of your turn, you need 3 arcane tokens at the start of your turn.  At the end of your turn H&M can set up your nest turn with a flip.  Uncontrolled Flock needs at least 1 Arcane token at the start of your turn or you lose it.

Darkwatch Harpy is much faster at swinging between Avian and Arcane.  You can flip a lot of tokens with that power and a second card play.  With DW Harpy you really need to strategically use your cards that flip tokens.  To get the most out of DW Harpy you need to plan out several potential turns that allow you to do different things and then when your turn comes up do the one that fits best.

Original Harpy is amazing with Applied Numerology, and your main power drives your deck.  With less token flipping you will often just sit on one side of the token spectrum, and won't bounce back and forth quite as much.  This one is less complex than DW, simply because Harpy will often feel like you don't have anything to do even though you have a ton of cards, if you aren't thinking ahead and setting up big swings and turns.

They tend to rely on particular rules that have evolved in importance over time - not sure whether that’s because the game evolved, or as more heroes entered the fray those rules became more relevant/got more of a focus. The best example is Benchmark (and I suspect Shipshape works like this, too): used to be that we’d treat it as players’ choice which order to activate the end of turn effects. Benchmark, though, RELIES ON effects occurring in the order the cards were played. It’s kind of neat how you have to set him up as a program to execute, but it involves the player keeping track of an element of the game that they don’t usually have to pay much attention to. (Now that I write it out, though, I see more value in him as adding something new to the game.)

I forgot to mention, in Oblivaeon games, Idealist goes from 'strong performer with some consistency issues' to potentially 'strongest hero in the game'.

So far I've played 6 games of Oblivaeon, and the Idealist, when paired with the mission reward from 'Form the MechaKnight', is the most powerful weapon in the hero's arsenel.

Even in the hands of another hero, the reward combines with damage boosting effects to do upwards of 11-16 damage per power use. In the hands of the Idealist, it allows her to hit multiple targets, potentially wiping out Scions as well as Oblivaeon. 

If you really want to cheese things out, you can also make sure the first hero everyone plays as each game have 'one hero may use a power' as one of their incapacitated abilities. Then, when Idealist has formed the Mechaknight, you can use your beginning of turn bonus action (the ones on the Hero Reminder Card) to use the incapacitated ability to allow Idealist to use her power.

Last game we had Idealist activating the MechaKnight power every hero turn, along with Legacy's galvanize and a +1 to all damage environment effect, to do 16 damage x 5 hero turns = 80 damage to multiple targets each round.

Dandolo:

I was the one pushing for the Shipshape effect in playtesting.

posts.name: Matchstickman
posts.cooked:
Thanks to Powerhound_2000 I found my posts on powercreep (which would be a pretty great name for a villain... just saying).

 

> I did some testing!

 

20 four-hero games vs Advanced Baron Blade in Insula Primalis, 10 games with just heroes from the base set and then 10 games with OblivAeon & Mini-Expansion heroes (no variants for either set).

 

On average they both took 5 turns to win.

 

The Base heroes did a tiny bit more damage than the OblivAeon heroes, but you would expect them to do roughly the same damage if pitted against the same deck again and again.

 

The OblivAeon heroes played roughly 100 more cards than the base heroes, and drew about 100 more cards too (311/210 and 300/198 respectively).

The OblivAeon heroes handed out almost 3 times as many powers to their friends (71/24).

Base heroes lost 2 games, OblivAeon heroes lost 1.

 

Counting losses as 4 heroes at 0HP the base heroes lost 9 members of their team over the 10 games and the OblivAeon heroes lost 6 heroes but the base heroes generally ended on higher HP when they won.

 

What does this mean?

Well, it appears to me that the OblivAeon heroes are doing more things, but the things they are doing are not more effective than the smaller number of things the base heroes are doing. It would appear the OP-ness is all in the mind (or I'm misinterpreting the data or the sample size is too small to draw any conclusions).

 

Google Doc with raw data if you want to see actual numbers.

 

Someone asked why I used this particular set up

> I wanted to compare a "pure" base set untainted by possible power creep from other expansions. The specifics choices were because Insula doesn't stop any action (draw, power etc) and Blade doesn't destroy your stuff so it's a pretty "friendly" combination for heroes to get set up. Blade still provides a time crunch on his front and a guaranteed DR on his back so you have to deal with both.

And that same someone suggested more testing against The Dreamer, Miss Information and Omnitron.

> The Dreamer (Standard) in Insula Primalis

Google Doc

I remember why I don't play The Dreamer much. Brutal openings and having to manage when to destroy targets so you don't lose your best stuff is brain draining when you're not trying to track everything too!

 

Both teams won more games than they lost, but the base heroes won more games overall and sacrificed themselves more often to accomplish it, guess that's why they're stalwalt heroes and the other lot are reforming villains.

 

More cycling of decks, more power granted and more cards played by the OblivAeon lot, but less damage overall (destruction of targets via e.g. Sucker Punch was counted as damage equal to the HP of the projection), so a similar lot of data to the first set.

When OblivAeon heroes did win, they were, on average, faster at it then base heroes. I don't know if that means that base heroes are more tanky and can survive earlier blitzs or if it means OblivAeon heroes can generate a lot more damage early if they get the right conditions, or both.

 

The last game however made up for all the pain I suffered playing and recording this match up. Luminary was "Hero" of the match, destroying all neccessary projections on The Dreamer's flip side with 2 Triple Crosses and finishing off with a Terralunar Translocator. Never has smashing a piece of the moon into a little girl been so satisfying.

I thought I did the Miss Information test too, but I can't find a spreadsheet on my HD, if I find it I'll edit this post with more thoughts and a link.

That's a cool comparison. It will be interesting to see how the statistics project eventually ranks the new heroes - but you've gone beyond that in tallying cards played and extra powers granted. I guess this data does feed into the idea that the new heroes are more complicated in that they have to set up more stuff in order to achieve the same effects.

I played another La Comodora game last night. "Shipshape" is definitely going into my default pile of cards to discard to keep her other equipment alive. I still can't see playing it: I realized that if I have equipment in the "wrong" order, playing "Shipshape" to reorder that equipment would force me to pay the upkeep twice on the reordered card. It's more efficient to just let some equipment vanish and play another copy of that same equipment. There just aren't enough copies of it in the deck for it to matter too much, though, so I can ignore my complaints.

What I find really interesting about La Comodora is how it doesn't feel like she's directly engaged in the battle. She's off behind the lines, providing direction and supporting effects. That's an awesome thing to come through in the mechanics for a ship captain! Man, can it feel like she has to sit through some turns of not doing much, though, as she gets set up. I suspect the only antidote to that feeling would be if you can play the Future-Tech Deck Gun on the first turn, so that she has a power she can use right away that doesn't rely on heroes having cards in their trash.

I think my wife and I both think Luminary is the most fun of the new heroes. (Stuntman is a close second, and I was surprised how much fun I found Mainstay.) He captures the mad scientist feel very well, and the doomsday device mechanic is awesome - unlike playing any of the other heroes who deploy targets, I have the most disposable attitude towards Luminary's devices. It really brings out the Ramonat in both of us. >:-D
